title: Ironbank Financial x Redwood — Technical deep dive: policy evaluation + latency
summary: Ironbank engineers drilled into Redwood RBAC v2 authorization evaluation location (gateway vs services), caching (TTL/invalidation), and the expected impact on p95/p99 latency for inference and control-plane APIs. Redwood described a deny-by-default model with endpoint annotations, an embedded evaluation client with scoped caching, and fail-closed semantics. Ironbank emphasized strict requirements for deterministic decisions, clear "why denied" feedback for admins, and SIEM-friendly audit logs including decision context and policy version.
topics: Where authorization checks run (API Gateway vs Control Plane services)
Policy evaluation design: embedded client vs centralized service
Caching strategy: TTL, invalidation on role/role-binding changes, safe scoping
Latency impact and p99 budget; what happens on cache misses
Failure modes: evaluator unavailable, partial outages, regional failover
Denial reason codes, debug headers, and "why was I denied" workflow
Audit log fields for authz decisions and SIEM export mapping
questions: Do authz checks run on every inference request, or only on control-plane/admin endpoints?
If the policy evaluator is slow or down, do you fail closed? Any break-glass exceptions?
How do you guarantee cache correctness when role bindings change?
What is the expected p99 latency add for gateway enforcement with cache hit vs miss?
Can we get denial reasons in a machine-readable way for support and internal tooling?
How is policy versioning represented in audit logs for evidence?
next_steps: Redwood to share written notes/diagram of evaluation flow (gateway -> service) and caching TTL/invalidation triggers.
Redwood to provide benchmark numbers for authz middleware overhead (cache hit/miss) and recommended TTL defaults for Private deployments.
Redwood to send sample audit log entries showing authz decision fields + SIEM-exported representation.
Ironbank to confirm scope model needed for their org/project/env separation and any constraints from their IdP group structure.
Schedule follow-up (45 min) to review Ironbank’s target request rates and align on which endpoints require per-request authz vs session-scoped checks.
action_items: Owner: Jordan Lee — Send evaluation flow diagram + notes on embedded client behavior and fail-closed semantics (by 2025-03-21).
Owner: Amara Diallo — Share latency overhead measurements and gateway middleware configuration options (by 2025-03-22).
Owner: Kevin Osei — Provide example audit logs with authz decision context + SIEM mapping fields (by 2025-03-22).
Owner: Maya Chen — Provide Ironbank’s p95/p99 latency budget + expected RBAC change frequency (roles/bindings) (by 2025-03-25).
transcript:
Meeting: Ironbank Financial x Redwood — Technical deep dive: policy evaluation + latency
Recorded: 2025-03-19 14:00 ET
Duration: 58 minutes

Attendees
Redwood Inference: Colin O'Donnell (SE / Solutions), Jordan Lee (Policy Engine), Amara Diallo (API Gateway), Kevin Osei (Audit Logs)
Ironbank Financial: Maya Chen (Staff Platform Eng), Raj Patel (Security Architect), Elena Morozova (SRE), Tom Gallagher (Eng Manager)

---

[00:00] Colin O'Donnell: Alright, cool. I think we’re all here. Thanks everybody. This one is meant to be pretty technical, like we can go straight into the weeds. The main themes you sent were, where authz runs, caching, and what the latency tax looks like.

[00:15] Tom Gallagher: Yep. Exactly. We’re trying to decide if we can put this in the critical path for some internal services without blowing our p99.

[00:22] Colin O'Donnell: Makes sense. I pulled in Jordan and Amara, and Kevin for the audit log angle.

[00:28] Raj Patel: Great.

[00:30] Colin O'Donnell: Before we jump, quick framing question. Are you mainly worried about inference requests, like token streaming endpoints, or control plane actions, like creating keys, changing routing policy, exporting logs, that sort of thing?

[00:44] Maya Chen: Both, but different constraints. For inference, we don’t want a centralized policy call on every request. For control plane, fine, but it still needs to be deterministic and fail-closed.

[00:57] Elena Morozova: And in our environment, we have like intermittent packet weirdness between clusters. So if it depends on a remote call, it’s… not great.

[01:07] Colin O'Donnell: Yep. Jordan, do you want to give the “where it runs” overview?

[01:11] Jordan Lee: Sure. So the design we’re implementing for RBAC v2 is, enforcement is deny-by-default at the edge for the API Gateway routes that are considered security-relevant, and then services also enforce for sensitive operations. We don’t rely on only one layer.

[01:28] Raj Patel: So double-enforcement.

[01:30] Jordan Lee: In a lot of cases, yes. Gateway is the first check to stop obvious unauthorized calls early, and services do a second check especially where there’s any chance of bypass, like internal routes, streaming handlers, async jobs, or anything that can be invoked outside the normal gateway path.

[01:46] Amara Diallo: And just to be clear, the gateway check is not calling out to an external “authz service” per request in the common path. It uses a local client with caching.

[01:56] Maya Chen: When you say “local client,” you mean a library in-process?

[02:00] Amara Diallo: Exactly. Library that evaluates based on the subject, action, resource scope, and a policy bundle version. It can fetch policy/bindings from the control plane but that is cached.

[02:12] Elena Morozova: So it’s still a remote fetch sometimes.

[02:15] Amara Diallo: On cache misses, yes. But the intent is to keep cache hit rate high and keep TTL safe.

[02:24] Tom Gallagher: Let’s anchor this. Suppose a user hits your inference chat endpoint, streaming. Does that require an authz evaluation every time?

[02:32] Colin O'Donnell: For most customers today, inference is authorized by API key. In RBAC v2, we’re still using the API key as the primary “can you call inference at all” gate, with quotas, etc. The RBAC v2 granularity is more for admin and control-plane actions—like who can rotate keys, who can change routing policy, who can export audit logs, manage org/users/roles.

[02:54] Maya Chen: Okay, so inference isn’t like “permission per prompt.”

[02:58] Colin O'Donnell: Correct. Not for the first phase. There are a couple of inference-adjacent operations—like changing model pinning or rollout policies—that are definitely RBAC-protected.

[03:09] Raj Patel: That’s fine. Our big concern is admin APIs and also the console, because we need separation of duties.

[03:17] Jordan Lee: Right, that’s the sweet spot for this design.

[03:20] Maya Chen: Can you describe the evaluation flow? Like what exactly is being computed and what are you caching?

[03:27] Jordan Lee: Sure. In abstract terms: subject (user or service principal), action (permission string), resource scope (org/project/env/cluster), and context like deployment mode, then we compute whether any role binding grants that permission at that scope or above.

[03:45] Maya Chen: And the scope hierarchy is like org > project > environment?

[03:50] Jordan Lee: That’s the model we’re implementing, with some nuances for Private where “cluster” scope can exist. Diego is not on this call but I can cover. The important piece for caching is that the decision is keyed by (subject_id, action, scope_id, policy_version-ish).

[04:10] Elena Morozova: “policy version-ish” meaning what exactly?

[04:13] Jordan Lee: Sorry. Meaning the evaluation depends on (1) role templates/permissions catalog version and (2) role bindings state. We expose policy bundle version for the templates, and we also include a “bindings revision” or “subject grants version” in cache keys, depending on where you run it.

[04:32] Raj Patel: Do you have an actual monotonic revision number for bindings?

[04:36] Jordan Lee: In control plane, yes, we can. At gateway, we can treat it as TTL-based plus invalidate-on-change via push or polling.

[04:46] Maya Chen: Okay, so let’s talk invalidation because TTL-only is where people get hurt.

[04:51] Jordan Lee: Agree. So the safe approach we’re taking: short TTL on allow decisions, even shorter on deny decisions, plus explicit invalidation triggers when role bindings change.

[05:05] Elena Morozova: Wait—why shorter on deny?

[05:07] Jordan Lee: Because if you just denied someone, and then an admin grants the permission, you don’t want them stuck getting denied for a long time. So deny TTL is typically like 5–15 seconds, allow TTL might be 30–60 seconds in hosted. For Private, operators can configure.

[05:24] Raj Patel: For us, the more dangerous one is the opposite: someone gets removed, but they retain access for up to 60 seconds.

[05:31] Jordan Lee: Totally fair. That’s why we pair TTL with invalidation. When a role binding is changed, we emit an event and invalidate caches for affected subjects.

[05:43] Maya Chen: Across a fleet.

[05:45] Jordan Lee: Yes. That’s the hard part. You can do targeted invalidation by subject ID. You can also bump a “subject grants version” stored centrally that the cache consults.

[05:57] Amara Diallo: In the gateway implementation, the practical model is: cache entries include a “grants_etag” we got from the evaluator. If we detect the grants_etag changed, we drop and re-fetch.

[06:10] Elena Morozova: That still requires checking the etag every request.

[06:14] Amara Diallo: Not necessarily. You can check etag on a cadence, like every N seconds, or piggyback on cache refresh. We’re trying to avoid per-request remote dependency.

[06:27] Tom Gallagher: What is the actual remote thing you’re calling? Is it a central policy service? Or the control plane DB?

[06:33] Jordan Lee: It’s a policy-evaluator endpoint in the control plane. It’s logically centralized, but we can deploy it regionally with the rest of the control plane. It’s not a database call from the gateway directly.

[06:46] Raj Patel: So it is centralized in the sense it’s one service.

[06:50] Jordan Lee: It is a service, yes. But we decided not to make it a hard dependency for the hot path by using caching and optional embedded evaluation for some workloads.

[07:00] Maya Chen: You said “optional embedded evaluation.” What does that mean?

[07:03] Jordan Lee: In some services, especially control plane services, we can embed the evaluator library and keep a local copy of bindings for that org/project, updated via watch. Then the evaluation is fully in-process.

[07:18] Elena Morozova: So like OPA sidecar but in-process.

[07:21] Jordan Lee: Kinda, yes, except the policy language is very constrained. It’s not general ABAC. It’s RBAC with scoping and some special cases.

[07:31] Raj Patel: That’s good. We don’t want a policy language for customers anyway.

[07:35] Colin O'Donnell: Yeah, that’s actually out-of-scope for v2, like end-user scripting.

[07:41] Maya Chen: Can we talk about the latency numbers? Like, what’s the p99 overhead of the gateway middleware on cache hit and miss.

[07:49] Amara Diallo: Sure. So, caveat: numbers vary by region and deployment. But in our internal benchmarks, cache-hit evaluation in gateway is sub-millisecond, usually 0.2–0.6 ms added, including permission lookup and decision formatting.

[08:06] Maya Chen: That’s acceptable.

[08:08] Amara Diallo: Cache miss requires a call to the evaluator endpoint. In-region that’s about 6–15 ms median, p99 can be 30–50 ms if the control plane is under load.

[08:22] Elena Morozova: That’s the scary case.

[08:24] Amara Diallo: Yes. Which is why the config goal is to avoid misses with pre-warming and safe TTL.

[08:32] Raj Patel: Do you do negative caching? Like cache denies?

[08:35] Amara Diallo: Yes, with short TTL, like Jordan mentioned.

[08:39] Maya Chen: In your design, can you prefetch the permissions for a given subject at login?

[08:45] Jordan Lee: We can. Console session can fetch a “grants snapshot” for the user, and then subsequent UI calls can have fewer misses. For API calls, it’s trickier, but for service-to-service or admin workflows, you can warm the cache by calling “whoami/permissions” type endpoints.

[09:05] Tom Gallagher: We’d prefer not to add extra calls.

[09:07] Colin O'Donnell: Understood. But note, most of the sensitive operations aren’t in a super-high-QPS path. Key rotation, role management, audit export. Those are not thousands per second.

[09:19] Elena Morozova: Some are bursty. Like routing policy edits can happen from automation.

[09:23] Jordan Lee: Routing policy edits are RBAC-protected, yes. But even there, you probably have tens per minute, not tens of thousands.

[09:34] Maya Chen: Let’s talk failure mode. If the evaluator is unreachable and the cache is cold, what happens?

[09:41] Jordan Lee: Fail closed. Deny-by-default. We return a 403 with a standardized error code.

[09:49] Raj Patel: That’s what we want for admin operations.

[09:51] Maya Chen: But then you’re coupling availability of control plane to the ability to administer.

[09:56] Jordan Lee: Yes. There are mitigations: caching, local embedded evaluation for private, and break-glass for emergency. But conceptually, yes, if you can’t evaluate policy, you can’t do sensitive stuff.

[10:10] Elena Morozova: How does break-glass work without becoming a huge hole.

[10:14] Colin O'Donnell: Break-glass is time-bound, heavily logged, and alerts SecOps. It’s not an automated bypass on the gateway. It’s an explicit role binding or token with an expiry.

[10:27] Raj Patel: Is it like AWS “assume role” with MFA.

[10:31] Colin O'Donnell: Similar spirit. For Private deployments, you can integrate with your IdP groups for the emergency group, with on-call procedures.

[10:40] Kevin Osei: And from logging standpoint, break-glass actions are tagged in the audit logs so you can prove usage and review after.

[10:48] Maya Chen: Okay. Now, on the cache correctness, I want to understand: if I remove a role binding for a user, what’s the maximum time they can still be authorized.

[10:59] Jordan Lee: With TTL-only, it’s TTL. With invalidation, it’s propagation delay plus any in-flight caches. In hosted we target seconds-level invalidation. In private it depends on the customer’s infra.

[11:14] Elena Morozova: “seconds-level” is vague.

[11:16] Jordan Lee: Fair. Our internal SLO target is <10 seconds to invalidate subject caches across a region after a binding change.

[11:25] Raj Patel: That might still be high for some privileged operations.

[11:28] Jordan Lee: If you have extremely privileged operations—like delete organization, export all audit logs, rotate root keys—those can require re-check with fresh grants, meaning we bypass cached allow and force a revalidation.

[11:45] Maya Chen: That’s good. So you have “freshness required” flags per permission?

[11:50] Jordan Lee: That’s a direction. Not all are implemented yet, but the pattern exists. Amara, in gateway, we can mark some endpoints as “no-cache allow.”

[12:00] Amara Diallo: Right. Endpoint annotations can specify cache behavior: normal, force-refresh, or deny-only cache.

[12:08] Tom Gallagher: Can you share that matrix? Like which actions require fresh check.

[12:12] Colin O'Donnell: We can send a list of “critical permissions” where we recommend forced refresh. It aligns with our test coverage set.

[12:20] Maya Chen: Now, what about streaming endpoints? We saw in another vendor once, streaming routes bypass middleware because of how the router was structured.

[12:29] Amara Diallo: Yeah, that can happen. Actually we had an internal issue like that earlier this quarter—streaming handler path wasn’t invoking the authz middleware due to a different code path. We fixed it and added a regression test.

[12:44] Raj Patel: Thanks for being candid. That’s exactly why service-level enforcement matters.

[12:48] Amara Diallo: Exactly.

[12:50] Maya Chen: Can you clarify what “permission string” looks like? Is it like “org.roles.update” or something.

[12:56] Jordan Lee: Yes, it’s namespaced and versioned. Example: “org.roles.write”, “audit.export.read”, “routing.policy.update”. We keep them stable and deprecate with a policy.

[13:10] Raj Patel: Versioned how? Like “routing.policy.update.v2”?

[13:14] Jordan Lee: We try not to encode version in the string unless necessary. More like keep the permission stable, and evolve behavior behind it carefully. If we truly need a breaking semantic shift, we can add a new permission and deprecate the old.

[13:28] Maya Chen: So for caching, the key includes “policy bundle version,” which is basically the catalog plus role templates.

[13:34] Jordan Lee: Exactly.

[13:36] Elena Morozova: Okay. Observability: how do I know when denies spike because of stale cache or policy mismatch.

[13:43] Amara Diallo: We emit metrics: allow/deny counters by permission, cache hit rate, evaluator latency, and a “stale grants detected” counter.

[13:55] Elena Morozova: Is that in Prometheus or your console.

[13:58] Colin O'Donnell: In hosted, it’s in our console plus we can export. In private, you can scrape metrics.

[14:06] Raj Patel: And audit logs: do you log every authorization decision, or only the sensitive actions.

[14:11] Kevin Osei: Great question. We log the decision context for security-relevant actions—basically anything that mutates state or exports sensitive data. We don’t log every inference call as an “authz decision,” but we do log admin actions, role changes, key operations, policy updates, audit exports.

[14:31] Maya Chen: What fields.

[14:33] Kevin Osei: Subject identifier, action/permission, scope, decision allow/deny, policy version identifiers, and if deny, a structured reason code. We can also include “evaluated_by” like gateway vs service.

[14:50] Raj Patel: Do you include “why” as a human message.

[14:53] Kevin Osei: We include a user-facing message but we’re careful. Typically it’s generic. For admins, you can request a debug header that includes additional details like “missing_permission” or “scope_mismatch.”

[15:07] Maya Chen: Debug header is only for admins.

[15:09] Kevin Osei: Correct, and it’s gated. Also gets logged.

[15:13] Elena Morozova: Nice.

[15:15] Tom Gallagher: Back to where enforcement happens. If the gateway enforces, and the service also enforces, are you doing two evaluator calls.

[15:25] Jordan Lee: Ideally no. The gateway can pass an “authz context” token downstream indicating which permission was checked and at what scope, and the service can accept it for low-risk endpoints.

[15:40] Raj Patel: That sounds like a new thing to trust.

[15:42] Jordan Lee: Exactly. That’s why for high-risk operations, the service still does its own check, not trusting the gateway. For medium-risk, we can reduce duplication.

[15:53] Maya Chen: Is that token signed.

[15:55] Jordan Lee: Yes, signed by the gateway, short-lived, and includes request hash to prevent replay across endpoints.

[16:07] Elena Morozova: Okay, that’s decent.

[16:09] Raj Patel: We’d likely require service enforcement for the top-tier actions anyway.

[16:13] Colin O'Donnell: That matches how most regulated customers do it.

[16:17] Maya Chen: How do you define sensitivity tiers.

[16:20] Jordan Lee: We classify permissions into tiers internally. Like tier 0 is org destroy / root-level, tier 1 is key management, audit export, role binding changes, tier 2 is read-only access to metadata. That classification informs defaults for caching and logging.

[16:40] Tom Gallagher: Good.

[16:42] Maya Chen: What about consistency between hosted, dedicated, private. We don’t want semantics to differ.

[16:49] Jordan Lee: Same semantics. The difference is deployment topology. In hosted/dedicated, evaluator service is part of Redwood control plane. In private, you run it inside your environment, and you can choose embedded evaluation in certain components for reliability.

[17:08] Elena Morozova: In private, can we run evaluator per cluster rather than central.

[17:12] Colin O'Donnell: Typically there’s a control plane cluster and then data plane clusters. Evaluator lives with control plane, but we can replicate or put read replicas close to data plane. This is something we’d design in the POC.

[17:28] Maya Chen: Okay. Another question: what’s the overhead of policy evaluation computation itself. Like number of roles, bindings, etc.

[17:37] Jordan Lee: The evaluation is basically set membership checks. We keep role -> permissions in memory, and bindings are indexed by subject and scope. Complexity is bounded. If someone has 100 roles and 1,000 bindings, you can get slower, but we enforce limits.

[17:55] Raj Patel: Limits are good.

[17:57] Maya Chen: Do you support group bindings.

[18:00] Jordan Lee: Yes. Users can have group claims from SSO, and you can bind roles to groups. The evaluator expands groups -> subjects.

[18:10] Raj Patel: Any issues with large group claim sets.

[18:13] Jordan Lee: There are practical limits. We recommend using a small number of coarse groups and then do fine-grained roles inside Redwood.

[18:24] Maya Chen: That’s tricky because our IdP team loves many groups.

[18:28] Raj Patel: (laughs) Yep.

[18:30] Colin O'Donnell: We can talk about best practices there. But the core evaluation supports it.

[18:37] Elena Morozova: On caching, what’s the default TTL you said. 60 seconds allow.

[18:41] Jordan Lee: That’s a placeholder example. We’re still tuning. In practice, we might go 30 seconds allow, 10 seconds deny for gateway.

[18:51] Elena Morozova: And invalidation within 10 seconds.

[18:53] Jordan Lee: Target.

[18:55] Maya Chen: Is there a “max stale” guarantee.

[18:58] Jordan Lee: We can provide a configuration for maximum staleness for allow decisions, yes. For tier-0 actions, max stale is effectively 0 because we refresh.

[19:10] Tom Gallagher: Okay. I want to sanity check: you’re not trying to run OPA in the gateway.

[19:15] Amara Diallo: No.

[19:16] Jordan Lee: No, we’re not doing general policy evaluation. It’s RBAC.

[19:20] Maya Chen: Good.

[19:22] Raj Patel: Can you explain denial reason codes. We need them for helpdesk.

[19:27] Kevin Osei: Yes. Typical codes: MISSING_PERMISSION, SCOPE_MISMATCH, SUBJECT_SUSPENDED, POLICY_NOT_FOUND (rare), EVALUATOR_UNAVAILABLE, and sometimes “TEMPLATE_DISABLED” when a permission is deprecated.

[19:45] Raj Patel: Do you expose EVALUATOR_UNAVAILABLE to the user.

[19:48] Kevin Osei: To the end user, we might still show “permission denied” but for admins or internal logs, we include the underlying code. We don’t want attackers to learn architecture.

[20:01] Maya Chen: That’s the right trade.

[20:03] Elena Morozova: For our SOC evidence, we need to show “who attempted what and was denied,” too.

[20:09] Kevin Osei: We log denies for these actions, yes.

[20:12] Raj Patel: And you can export to SIEM.

[20:14] Kevin Osei: Yes. Our exporter maps the fields to common SIEM schema conventions. We can send examples.

[20:22] Colin O'Donnell: Maybe we pivot to an example flow. Maya, give me a concrete operation you care about, and we’ll walk through it.

[20:29] Maya Chen: Okay. “Dedicated admin edits routing policy” — like change which model version is pinned for an environment.

[20:37] Jordan Lee: Great. So request hits gateway route PATCH /routing/policies/{id}. Endpoint annotated with permission ROUTING_POLICY_UPDATE (name simplified). Gateway extracts subject from authn (SSO or API token), resolves scope: org + project + environment.

[20:57] Amara Diallo: Gateway calls local evaluator client. Cache lookup: key(subject, permission, scope). If hit allow, continue. If miss, call evaluator endpoint to fetch subject grants and compute decision.

[21:13] Jordan Lee: Then gateway passes request to control plane routing service. Routing service does its own check because it’s a sensitive mutation. It can either re-evaluate with embedded library or call evaluator; typically it uses the same client library with caching.

[21:32] Elena Morozova: So two caches.

[21:34] Jordan Lee: Correct.

[21:36] Maya Chen: That means two potential misses.

[21:38] Jordan Lee: It does, but misses are rare after warmup. And for these operations, the overall latency isn’t in the single-digit ms anyway.

[21:49] Tom Gallagher: Our internal automation does a bunch of these changes during deployments.

[21:55] Jordan Lee: Understood. For automation, we recommend a service principal with stable grants, and you’ll get high cache hit rates.

[22:05] Raj Patel: Are service principals distinct from users.

[22:08] Jordan Lee: Yes. They’re subjects with their own bindings.

[22:11] Maya Chen: Okay. Another example: “export audit logs.” That’s the one where you really don’t want stale access.

[22:19] Kevin Osei: Exactly. For audit export, we likely mark it as tier 0 or tier 1. The service would force a fresh evaluation or require a grants_etag match to current revision.

[22:34] Raj Patel: Good.

[22:36] Elena Morozova: Are you logging the authorization decision in the audit log itself. That feels meta.

[22:42] Kevin Osei: Yes, ironically. The audit event for “AUDIT_EXPORT_REQUESTED” includes “authz_decision=allow” and policy versions.

[22:51] Elena Morozova: That’s great.

[22:53] Tom Gallagher: Ok switching: we also care about latency on console. If I load the roles page and it triggers 30 calls, does each call require authz.

[23:02] Colin O'Donnell: Console backend does checks, but the UI is designed to minimize chatter. Also, there’s a concept of “permission viewer” endpoint where it fetches your effective permissions once.

[23:13] Maya Chen: But still, each API call is separately authorized.

[23:17] Jordan Lee: Correct. We don’t want UI to be trusted.

[23:20] Raj Patel: Good.

[23:22] Maya Chen: What about “why was I denied” UX. How does that work without leaking too much.

[23:28] Kevin Osei: The standard response is 403 with an error code. If you’re an org admin or security admin, you can include a header like X-Redwood-Debug-Authz: true, and then you get a denial reason code and the missing permission string. That’s logged.

[23:49] Maya Chen: If I’m not admin, I get generic.

[23:52] Kevin Osei: Exactly.

[23:54] Elena Morozova: Is there a support workflow where we can tell a user exactly which role to request.

[23:59] Colin O'Donnell: Yes, we have role templates like “Read-only auditor,” “Security admin,” “Deployment operator.” Those map to sets of permissions. But you can also create custom roles.

[24:10] Raj Patel: We like templates as a starting point.

[24:13] Tom Gallagher: You mentioned policy bundle. Is that like a YAML file.

[24:18] Jordan Lee: Internally yes, role templates are defined declaratively and we publish a versioned bundle artifact consumed by services.

[24:28] Maya Chen: Does the bundle include customer custom roles.

[24:31] Jordan Lee: No, the bundle is templates and permission registry. Customer-defined roles and bindings are stored in control plane data store.

[24:41] Elena Morozova: Ok.

[24:42] Maya Chen: What about eventual consistency. If I create a role and immediately assign and call, do I get weird denies.

[24:50] Jordan Lee: There can be a short propagation delay. We’re trying to make it near-immediate in a region. The UI will generally wait for confirmation. And caches are invalidated on binding changes.

[25:06] Raj Patel: Any known issues there.

[25:09] Jordan Lee: Not “known knowns,” but we monitor denial spikes after role changes, and we have rollback flags during rollout.

[25:17] Maya Chen: Okay. Let me ask about competitor architecture. We’ve used AWS IAM and you call AWS STS etc. That’s centralized but extremely reliable. How do you reach that reliability.

[25:31] Colin O'Donnell: For hosted/dedicated, it’s our job to run it. For private, you own the infra but we ship defaults. Jordan’s team is designing it to be low CPU, low memory, and cache-friendly.

[25:45] Jordan Lee: Also, we deliberately kept the model simple so evaluator can be very reliable.

[25:52] Elena Morozova: In private, can we put evaluator behind a local service mesh and do retries.

[25:57] Amara Diallo: Yes. But keep in mind, retries add latency. Better to increase cache TTL slightly and improve invalidation.

[26:05] Elena Morozova: Right.

[26:07] Maya Chen: Another question: do you sign the policy bundle so we can attest to what rules were in effect.

[26:14] Jordan Lee: The bundle is versioned and we can sign it. Audit logs include the bundle version. So for evidence, you can say “on date X, decision was made under policy bundle v2025.03.18” etc.

[26:30] Raj Patel: That’s important for our auditors.

[26:33] Kevin Osei: We can provide an “evidence pack” type export with sample logs and version attestation.

[26:39] Tom Gallagher: Great.

[26:41] Maya Chen: Okay, let’s push on latency again. You said cache miss can be 30-50ms p99. How do we ensure we don’t see a lot of misses.

[26:50] Amara Diallo: Three levers: (1) warm caches at gateway startup with common permissions; (2) keep TTL not too low; (3) avoid per-endpoint unique permissions when possible—reuse permissions so cache keys are reused.

[27:10] Maya Chen: But reuse reduces granularity.

[27:12] Jordan Lee: You can still have granularity where it matters. But yes, there’s a balance.

[27:18] Raj Patel: We prefer granularity. Latency is secondary for admin operations.

[27:22] Tom Gallagher: For automation though, it’s more frequent.

[27:25] Jordan Lee: For automation we can provide a “bulk decision” endpoint. Like evaluate multiple permissions in one call, then cache.

[27:34] Maya Chen: That’s interesting.

[27:36] Elena Morozova: But then you need to trust the cached results.
